title: Why God came as Chaitanya
hookLine: does God ever feel what we feel? a book about a singer opens with its answer
carry: bhakti: love God longs to feel from our side
tomorrow: a stranger faints in a temple. who carries him home?

lines: DOES GOD FEEL WHAT WE FEEL?
YES. HE CAME TO FIND OUT.
cards: A little kid asks it at dinner, out of nowhere: does God ever feel what we feel? The grown-ups look at each other. It's a real question, and one old Hindu book builds its whole opening on an answer.
The book is the Chaitanya Charitamrita. And in its telling, the answer is yes: God wanted to know what loving God feels like, enough to come and find out.

teach.b: The book is about Chaitanya, a singer of Krishna's names. Charita is a life story; amrita is nectar. Its opening verses ask who he really was, and answer, in paraphrase: Radha and Krishna are one soul.
For the play of love they became two. Now they've appeared as one again, in Chaitanya, with Radha's feeling and Radha's golden color.
That's why the book calls him Gaura, the golden one. Then the reason. Krishna wanted to know how great Radha's love is, what wonder she tastes in him, and what joy she feels in loving him.
He couldn't know it from his own side.
So, the book says, he came with her heart. In this telling, bhakti isn't only a person reaching for God. God wants to know what the reaching feels like.
That's the Gaudiya Vaishnava answer, from the tradition that follows Chaitanya; other Hindus remember him as a devotee who filled the streets with Krishna's names.
A neighbor tradition has its own line about love that doesn't start on the human side.
In the First Epistle of John, Christians read: “We love him, because he first loved us.”
Shared: love between God and people runs both ways, and God isn't standing still at the far end. And an honest difference. In John's letter, God's love comes first and people answer it.
In the Charitamrita, Krishna comes to taste the answering side, the devotee's love, from inside it.

how: Gaudiya Vaishnavas read the Chaitanya Charitamrita as the life of Chaitanya and sing his and Krishna's names in kirtan; the opening verses on Radha and Krishna are recited in their worship and study.

games.q: a friend from a Christian family hears this and says, 'so it's the same as he first loved us, right?' what's the fair answer?
o: close but not the same: in John, God loves first; in the Charitamrita, Krishna tastes the devotee's side.
yes. it's exactly the same idea in different words.
no. the two have nothing in common at all.
games.why: shared: God isn't standing still at the far end of love. different: in 1 John, God's love comes first and people answer; in the Charitamrita, Krishna comes to taste the answering love itself.

practice: Find a photo of someone you love, on your phone or on a wall, or simply bring their face to mind. Look at it for the whole sit, and wonder what your love looks like from their side. Let the breath stay easy while you look.
